hints: Look first at the flat plateau on the right of Fig. 2.1. What value on the y-axis does the rate level off at, and what does that plateau tell you?
Now halve that maximum rate value and trace horizontally across to the curve, then straight down to the x-axis. What substrate concentration do you land on?
walkthrough:
Find Vmax From the Plateau**
Think of Vmax as the speed limit when every active site is working as fast as it can. On Fig. 2.1 the curve flattens at the top because active sites are saturated. Read across from that plateau to the y-axis and you get about $14 \mu mol \, dm^{-3} \, min^{-1}$.

Use Half Vmax to Find Km**
By definition, $K_m$ is the substrate concentration that gives half of Vmax. Half of 14 is 7, so find $7 \mu mol \, dm^{-3} \, min^{-1}$ on the y-axis, move across to the curve, then drop vertically down to the x-axis. You meet the x-axis at $0.3 \, mmol \, dm^{-3}$, which is the $K_m$.

Final answer: Vmax = $14 \mu mol \, dm^{-3} \, min^{-1}$. Half Vmax = $7 \mu mol \, dm^{-3} \, min^{-1}$. Km is the substrate concentration giving half Vmax, read from the x-axis as $0.3 \, mmol \, dm^{-3}$.

hints: Recall what a small Km versus a large Km tells you about how easily the enzyme grabs its substrate at low concentration.
If one enzyme needs more substrate to get to half its top speed, what does that say about its active site fit and how often enzyme-substrate complexes form?
walkthrough:
Link Km to Affinity**
Affinity means how readily the active site binds substrate to form an enzyme-substrate complex. A low Km means half Vmax is reached with only a little substrate, so affinity is high. A high Km means a lot more substrate is needed, so affinity is low. Enzyme B has the higher Km, so enzyme B has lower affinity than enzyme A.

Explain What Higher Km Means in Practice**
Because the fit between substrate and the active site of B is less effective, fewer collisions lead to complexes per unit time at any low substrate concentration. You therefore have to raise substrate concentration higher for B than for A to get to half Vmax. In a cell, A would be saturated and working steadily while B would still be sensitive to changes in substrate concentration.

Final answer: Enzyme B has a higher Km so has a lower affinity for substrate than enzyme A. Enzyme B needs a higher substrate concentration to reach half Vmax / to form enzyme-substrate complexes at the same rate.

hints: Picture where a competitive inhibitor fits. Which part of the enzyme does it block, and what does that do to the chance of a substrate landing there?
Think about low substrate concentration with lots of inhibitor around versus very high substrate concentration. Who wins the competition in each case?
If the inhibitor can be outcompeted at very high substrate levels, what will happen to the final top rate, Vmax?
If you need extra substrate just to get back to half speed, what must happen to the Km value?
walkthrough:
Block the Active Site**
A competitive inhibitor has a shape similar to the substrate, so it fits into the active site and competes with substrate for that space. While it sits there, substrate cannot bind, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time.

Slow Down at Low Substrate Concentration**
At low substrate concentration the inhibitor wins many of these contests, so the observed rate is lower than without inhibitor. On a rate against substrate graph the whole curve sits lower and to the right.

Outcompete at High Substrate Concentration**
This block is reversible, not permanent. If you flood the mixture with substrate, substrate molecules collide so much more often that they occupy almost all active sites. All enzymes can still be saturated, so the same Vmax of $14 \mu mol \, dm^{-3} \, min^{-1}$ is eventually reached. Vmax depends on enzyme concentration, which has not changed.

Explain the Higher Km**
Km is the substrate concentration needed for half Vmax. Because some active sites are tied up by inhibitor, you need a higher substrate concentration than $0.3 \, mmol \, dm^{-3}$ to get to $7 \mu mol \, dm^{-3} \, min^{-1}$. A larger substrate concentration for half Vmax means a larger Km.

Final answer: Competitive inhibitor occupies / blocks the active site, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and rate is lower at low substrate concentration, so curve is shifted right. At high substrate concentration substrate outcompetes inhibitor so Vmax is unchanged. More substrate is needed to reach half Vmax so Km is higher.
